1.grade_fit_note: School subjects lowercase except languages; a classic grade 5-6 capitalization error.
1.note: Clean 2x2 (Math/math x History/history); French is capitalized in every option so it is a fair constant. Sound item.

2.grade_fit_note: Nationality/language adjectives are a grade 3-4 skill but still a common slip; on the easy side for grade 5.
2.note: Both features are 'capitalize the proper adjective/noun', so the key is the most-capitalized option; a student who knows either half gets it. Easy but valid.

3.grade_fit_note: Generic 'middle school' vs historical period 'Middle Ages' is a good grade 6 contrast.
3.note: Well built: the two features pull in opposite directions (one lowercase, one capital), so no 'most/fewest capitals' heuristic works.

4.grade_fit_note: Agreement across an intervening prepositional phrase and relative clause, plus 'each ... has' — grade 6-7.
4.note: Sound. Distractor A (both plural) is the attractive all-wrong option because 'photos'/'grandparents'/'pictures' sit next to the verbs.

5.grade_fit_note: Inappropriate shift in mood (imperative to modal/indicative), L.8.1d / L.8.3a.
5.note: Key is noticeably the shortest option (it simply omits both 'you should' and 'you will'); a 'shortest is cleanest' guesser gets it. 'You will read each question twice' is a grammatical instruction in isolation, so the item tests consistency rather than grammaticality, which is fine for L.8.

6.grade_fit_note: Semicolon joining independent clauses vs comma after an introductory clause; CCSS places semicolons at L.9-10 but they are routinely taught by grade 8.
6.note: Sound 2x2. B (comma splice) is the strongest distractor; A and D test misuse of a semicolon after a dependent clause.

7.grade_fit_note: Possessive 'else's' and possessive pronoun 'ours' without an apostrophe are grade 4-6 skills.
7.note: Valid. 'our's' is a common enough error that the distractors are live, but a grade 7 target is a step high.

8.free_elimination: C and D can be killed by a symmetry instinct alone (a comma on only one side of the parenthetical looks lopsided), leaving A vs B.
8.note: Correct and clear. The mismatched options are weak because paired punctuation almost always matches; the real test is A vs B.

9.grade_fit_note: Past unreal conditional / 'would have' in the if-clause, L.8.1c.
9.note: Sound; 'last Saturday' anchors the past so D's 'would pack' is clearly wrong. B is the strong distractor (very common spoken form).

10.grade_fit_note: Gerund vs infinitive after stop/forget (meaning change), verbals L.8.1a.
10.note: All four options are grammatical strings; the wrong ones are wrong only by meaning in context ('stopped to talk' after a request for quiet, 'forgotten turning off' when it rang). Defensible, but it is really a semantics item and favours native speakers; strand label 'Parts of Speech' is loose.

11.grade_fit_note: Commas around a nonrestrictive appositive; grade 5-6.
11.free_elimination: B and D can be killed by symmetry alone (one comma of a pair), leaving A vs C.
11.note: Valid. Same paired-mark weakness as item 8.

12.grade_fit_note: Tag question and direct address, exactly L.5.2c.
12.note: Well aligned. A (period after a tag question) is a plausible but weaker lure; both features are independent.

13.note: Sound 2x2; 'sitting in math class, his stomach' is a subtler dangler than 'Running for the bus, his lunch', which is good spread.

14.grade_fit_note: Quotation marks for song and poem titles, L.5.2d.
14.note: Valid; italics are not available so quotes are the only marking. Easy once a student knows one title gets quotes, since both titles follow the same rule (key = most-marked).

15.grade_fit_note: Redundant conjunction (although...but) and double subject; grade 6-7.
15.note: Key is the shortest option (deletes both redundancies), same shape as item 5. Strand label 'Parts of Speech' is a stretch; this is sentence structure.

16.grade_fit_note: Colon after an independent clause, not after a linking verb; grade 7-8.
16.note: Key is correct but stylistically clunky: a colon list followed by ', and their main jobs...' lets the second clause read as part of the list. Consider ending the list sentence and starting a new one.

17.grade_fit_note: Pronoun shift in number/person, L.6.1d, but these shifts are glaring.
17.note: 'most of them take out your phones' is so unnatural that few grade 6 students would choose it, which kills B and C and leaves only A vs D.

18.grade_fit_note: Pronoun case in compound object and subject, L.6.1a.
18.note: Strong item: the key mixes object and subject forms, so a 'make them match' heuristic fails, and C targets the 'Priya and I' hypercorrection.

19.grade_fit_note: Past perfect for the earlier past action, L.5.1b-c.
19.note: Valid. A 'keep the two verbs parallel' instinct narrows to B or D (both consistent), so it is effectively a had/has decision.

20.note: Sound; the key has the fewest capitals. Easy end of grade 5.

21.note: Correct; 'long, windy' passes the reversal/and test, 'three old red' does not. Some editors tolerate omitting the comma between two short coordinate adjectives, but not as a mainstream rule.

22.note: Good contrast (opposite directions for the two features). AP and Chicago both capitalize 'the Southwest' as a region.

23.grade_fit_note: Title capitalization of short verbs/pronouns ('Is', 'It'); grade 6-7.
23.note: Valid under AP, Chicago and MLA title case (all capitalize 'Is' and 'It'). Both features follow the same rule, so the key is the most-capitalized option.

24.grade_fit_note: Cumulative adjectives take no comma, L.7.2a.
24.note: Sound; the constant 'tired, hungry' models the coordinate case. Key has the fewest commas, both features being 'no comma'.

25.grade_fit_note: Correlative 'neither...nor' with proximity agreement, L.5.1e; agreement half is hard for grade 5.
25.note: Correct by the proximity rule; B ('know') is widely heard and some usage notes tolerate notional plural, but mainstream guides want 'knows'. Minor: 'knows ... asked' is a tense mismatch present in every option.

26.grade_fit_note: Full names of a school and park are capitalized; grade 3-4 skill.
26.note: Valid but easy; both features follow the same rule, so the key is the most-capitalized option.

27.grade_fit_note: Comma after an introductory dependent clause, L.5.2b.
27.note: Sound. B (no comma) is the realistic distractor; C and D, which cut 'storm' from its verb, are weak but not dead for grade 5.

28.grade_fit_note: Paired dashes around an interrupting independent clause, L.8.2a.
28.free_elimination: C and D (mismatched comma/dash) can be killed by symmetry alone, leaving A vs B.
28.note: Correct; B is the good distractor (commas cannot set off a full independent clause). Paired-mark symmetry halves it.

29.note: Valid; 'myself' as subject is a live error, 'hisself' is non-standard but heard in some dialects, so neither is dead.

30.grade_fit_note: Restrictive 'that' clause vs nonrestrictive 'which' clause, L.6.2a / L.7.
30.note: Correct. 'which' refers to a whole clause, which some style guides call vague, but it is in every option and is standard usage.

31.grade_fit_note: Irregular past participles with present perfect, L.5.1b.
31.note: Sound; 'has swam' and 'has broke' are both common spoken errors, so all distractors are live.

32.grade_fit_note: Days of the week capitalized, 'weekend' lowercase: a grade 2-3 skill.
32.note: Valid but well below grade 5; 'sundays' lowercase is unlikely to tempt a fifth grader.

_batch.Spelling: No items in this batch are labeled Spelling (the strands present are Capitalization, Punctuation, 'Phrases, Clauses, Agreement, Sentences', and 'Parts of Speech'), so there is nothing to assess; note that the batch therefore does not cover the spelling standard it claims to align to.
_batch.Punctuation: All 12 items (6, 7, 8, 11, 12, 14, 16, 21, 24, 27, 28, 30) are 2x2 factorial designs with keys spread A3/B3/C3/D3, and mark counts do not predict the key (fewest marks in 8 and 24, most in 11, 12 and 14, middle in 16, 21, 27 and 30), so there is no position, length or count tell. The one recurring pattern is in paired-punctuation items 8, 11 and 28: the two options with a mismatched pair (a comma or dash on one side only) can be killed by symmetry alone. That leaves the key against the all-wrong option (none/both in 8 and 11, comma-comma in 28), so it halves the item but does not solve it.
_batch.Grammar and Usage: Covering the 12 'Phrases, Clauses...' and 'Parts of Speech' items (4, 5, 9, 10, 13, 15, 17, 18, 19, 25, 29, 31): all are 2x2, with keys spread A3/B3/C3/D3. Two weak cross-item tells exist. In redundancy items 5 and 15 the key is the shortest option, since it just deletes the extra words. In 4, 17 and 19 a 'make both verbs/pronouns match' heuristic narrows to the two internally consistent options (key plus the all-wrong option). Item 18 deliberately breaks the matching heuristic (key 'me ... she and I'), which is good. Item 17's 'your phones' options are implausible enough to be dead. Neither pattern holds across the strand strongly enough to guess from.
_batch.Capitalization: All 8 items (1, 2, 3, 20, 22, 23, 26, 32) are 2x2 with keys spread A2/B2/C2/D2. Capital count does not predict the key overall: fewest in 1 and 20, most in 2, 23 and 26, middle in 3, 22 and 32. But within an item, when both features follow the same direction (2, 23, 26 both capitalize; 1, 20 both lowercase), a student who knows either feature can pick the extreme-count option. Items 3, 22 and 32, with one feature each way, are better built. Several items (26, 32, and to a lesser degree 2 and 20) sit below their grade 5 target.
